title: Trans runner Nikki Hiltz upsets Faith Kipyegon at Pre Classic: ‘We’re not these big, scary things’
content:
EUGENE, Ore. — American Nikki Hiltz blazed to a first-place finish in the women’s mile Saturday at the Prefontaine Classic track meet, surging ahead of three-time Olympic gold medalist Faith Kipyegon down the stretch to post the best time in the world this season.

Hiltz crossed the finish line in 4 minutes, 17.49 seconds, as Kipyegon lost a race at a mile or 1,500 meters for the first time in five years. She ended up finishing third at 4:17.80, behind fellow Kenyan Dorcus Ewoi, who ran a personal best 4:17.62.

While Saturday’s victory was far from the 2024 Olympian’s first, it carried a little more weight in the wake of this week’s Supreme Court decision upholding state bans on transgender women and girls competing against cisgender women and girls in sports.

Hiltz competes in women’s events, but identifies as non-binary and transgender, using they/them pronouns. Hiltz said their win Saturday “totally” meant more — and not just because they finally got the opportunity to out-kick Kipyegon.

“I wasn’t surprised, but I was obviously still disappointed (in the Supreme Court ruling),” Hiltz said. “For me, I want to show that trans people can be in sport, be affirmed in their gender. We’re not these big, scary things.”

Transgender athletes have become a polarizing topic across the country in recent years. Shortly after taking office for his second term as president, Donald Trump signed an executive order to stop trans athletes from competing in girls’ and women’s sports unless they were assigned female at birth.

Twenty-seven states currently have laws banning trans girls and women from participating against cisgender women and girls. While the Supreme Court ruling focused specifically on cases in West Virginia and Idaho, it is expected to have far-reaching implications for those additional 25 states — and possibly more if other states pursue similar legislation.

Hiltz said they typically stay off social media on race week, meaning they didn’t see — or read — anyone gloating about the ruling. Instead, they focus on “just trying to show up as myself and maybe educate people along the way.”

“It’s a really weird time in our country for a lot of different communities, mine specifically,” Hiltz said.

Hiltz joked that it’s not uncommon for people to misgender them — or even understand what non-binary means.

“I get it from both sides,” Hiltz said, laughing. “People think I’m a trans man that’s taking testosterone, and I’m like, ‘No, I’m not doing that.’ Then I definitely get it the other way: They think I’m a biological man competing in women’s sports. And I’m like, ‘No, I’m not a trans woman either.’ Honestly, a lot of people can’t really even insult me correctly.”

The mile is not typically contested in high-profile track meets. But the Bowerman Mile — the men’s race named after the late Bill Bowerman, a longtime Oregon coach who mentored Steve Prefontaine, for whom the meet is named — is a staple of the Pre Classic. Saturday marked the first time since 1993 that there was a women’s mile race at the Pre, which Hiltz referred to as a “very American distance.”

The meet is a made-for-TV event. Like many Diamond League events, most races feature only finals and no qualifying heats. Athletes are often escorted to the starting line by a local kid at the meet. Hiltz said at the 2025 Pre, their “little buddy” told Hiltz, “I’m non-binary, I use they/them pronouns, I live in Eugene.”

“I was like, that’s so cool!” Hiltz recalled. “Trans kids are everywhere … you see all these headlines, but when you see face-to-face a kid who’s like, ‘This is how I identify,’ it can break your heart but also fill you with joy because I’m so glad you can be who you are at such a young age.”

Hiltz finished seventh in the 1,500 meters at the 2024 Paris Olympics and fifth in the same race at the 2025 world championships in Tokyo.

They will have more opportunities to represent trans athletes on the national stage later this month when Hiltz competes in the USATF national championships at Icahn Stadium in New York City. (They’re still determining which event they’ll compete in.)

Hiltz came out in 2021 and said it’s “night and day” compared to now in terms of how people in the track community — fellow athletes, coaches, broadcasters, etc. — “constantly reaffirm” who they are. Hiltz gushed about how other athletes will correct anyone who misgenders Hiltz.

“People just, I think, needed a few years or few months or whatever to learn,” they said. “But now it’s so normalized, and that’s so special to me — but not only to me, to any non-binary person or trans person tuning in to watch a race. They can see, ‘Oh, there’s someone who looks like me and is getting their pronouns respected.’

“That’s huge to combat everything that’s going on. I think the biggest thing is that right now, trans people are being dehumanized. I’m kind of doing the opposite, humanizing the (trans) experience. I think that can go a really long way.”
